memory: I can see that you're a Computer Science major in your fourth year. It sounds like you have a busy schedule this semester. You're finally taking higher-level courses that seemed far off when you were a freshman. It's surreal to be at this stage, isn't it? It feels like just yesterday you were in an intro class learning about simple data structures. Now you're diving into complex algorithmic concepts, advanced system design, and even quantum computing basics. How's it going so far?Your favorite class this semester is Advanced Algorithms. You enjoy how it connects theory to real-world problem-solving, like optimizing pathfinding in large networks or finding the fastest way to handle huge datasets with minimal time complexity. The class covers dynamic programming approaches and approximation algorithms for NP-hard problems, which can be mind-bending. Your professor is great at explaining these complex concepts in an intuitive way. She'll present a problem that seems impossible to solve in polynomial time and then show you a strategy to approximate a solution. You always leave the class with your mind buzzing. How does it feel to be learning these advanced concepts?Aside from Advanced Algorithms, your second most challenging course is Distributed Systems(CS 2631). It involves a lot of reading, group discussions, and a major project that simulates a decentralized file storage system. The group project is an adventure in itself. You have to collaborate with people who have different coding styles and sometimes different ideas about the final product. However, that's also the beauty of it. In real-world settings, you're never working in a vacuum. You have to be able to integrate your code with others' and handle issues like concurrency and node failures. It can be nerve-wracking at times, like when you spent hours troubleshooting a weird bug that turned out to be a misplaced bracket in one of the config files. But once you fixed it and everything ran smoothly, it was a huge sense of accomplishment. How do you find the experience of working on this project?You're also taking an elective in Game Design, which counts toward your major if you combine it with other specific classes. As a gamer at heart, this was a must-take for you. Your professor is from the industry and has worked on a couple of indie games that did well. You're learning about basic 2D and 3D engines, implementing physics, and even some user experience design. It's incredibly fun because every assignment is super creative. In your last assignment, you had to design a mini-game based on a labyrinth concept, focusing on balancing the difficulty curve so players wouldn't get frustrated and quit. It was challenging, but it was also rewarding to see it come together. How do you find the experience of learning game design?You also mentioned taking an Introduction to Quantum Computing class, which initially intimidated you but has turned out to be enjoyable. The professor focuses on conceptual understanding rather than pure math, which makes it more accessible. Of course, there is math involved, such as linear algebra, but it's balanced with code examples in frameworks that simulate quantum circuits. You're not building actual quantum computers, but you're modeling algorithms like Grover's and Shor's to see how they outperform classical methods. It's mind-blowing and has changed the way you approach problems. How has this class impacted your perspective on computing?You're also taking a Capstone Project course, which is essentially the sink-or-swim part of senior year. You have the entire semester to conceptualize, design, and build a software solution that solves a real problem. Your group decided to work on a project that uses machine learning to analyze social media sentiment for better emergency response. It involves reading a firehose of tweets or posts and analyzing them for words that might suggest a disaster or crisis. You're building an interface that city officials or campus security could use to see real-time alerts. This project is pulling together everything you've learned as a CS major, including database management, API building, front-end interface, and ML pipeline. Additionally, you're learning about project management and staying organized. One person on your team is the designated Scrum Master, so you have sprints and daily stand-ups every week. It's a lot, but if you can pull it off, you'll be incredibly proud. How's the project going so far?You're also taking a humanities elective called Philosophy of Mind. It's your last required non-CS elective, and you chose it because it ties into AI in interesting ways. You discuss consciousness, the concept of mind, and how it applies to artificial intelligence. The class is smaller, so there are a lot of class discussions, which is a welcome change from the coding in your other classes. It's nice to sit back and analyze abstract ideas sometimes. This class also helps you see the bigger picture, like the ethical implications of building AI systems that could mimic or simulate human thinking. You recently wrote a paper on whether strong AI could ever truly experience qualia, like the subjective experience of color or pain. It's a huge topic in the philosophy world, and researching it was fascinating. You believe bridging technical knowledge with ethical considerations is important, and this class provides that perspective. How do you find this class?Your schedule is quite packed, as is typical for a college student. Mondays and Wednesdays are the busiest days. You start with Advanced Algorithms at 9:30 am, followed by a short break before your Distributed Systems lecture at 11:00 am. After lunch, you have the Capstone meeting, which can be a mix of lectures, lab work, and project team time. Tuesdays and Thursdays are a bit lighter, with Quantum Computing in the morning and Game Design in the afternoon. Philosophy of Mind is on Thursday evenings, which can be tough if you're already tired from the rest of the day. Fridays are open, but you usually end up working on assignments, group projects, or labs. You also do research hours in a lab focused on data visualization for big scientific data sets. It's interesting, but it definitely adds to your workload. How do you manage to balance everything?The biggest challenge this semester is balancing the group projects. The Capstone project alone can consume around ten hours a week, and it can be even more time-consuming if you encounter a major bug or if your model isn't training properly. Additionally, the Distributed Systems project is another significant time-sink. Your group meets at least twice a week and relies on Slack or Discord to stay updated. Coordinating five different people's schedules can be a logistical nightmare. Despite the stress, it's also exciting. This is one of your last chances to fully invest in an academic project without the pressures of a job environment. How do you find the experience of working on these projects?Overall, you're having a great time. You used to dread the tougher CS classes because you were worried you wouldn't keep up, but now you've become better at problem-solving and time management. You still have the occasional late night, especially when something's due the next day and you're stuck debugging. However, it's no longer as scary as it used to be. Being a senior has given you confidence; you know that if you put in the effort and keep your eye on the end goal, you'll figure things out. The biggest takeaway is that after four years, you've learned to be resourceful, collaborate effectively, and think critically. These classes are tough, but they're also super rewarding. Everything you're doing now feels like it's directly building towards your future career, and that's a great feeling.
